Mr. Speaker, I raise a question of privilege.

All the newspapers which were good enough to report this speech of mine printed exactly what I said. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Last week, Mr. Speaker, we received this second note from the state department of the United States making the request which I have just mentioned. Naturally the Canadian government has given careful consideration to the second request, as it did, indeed, to the first one, having regard to the responsibilities that had been assumed and the special arrangements that have been carefully built up over the past several years for the safety of Mr. Gouzenko and leading to the development of a new identity; arrangements which would obviously not be effective if that new identity became public knowledge.
Mr. Gouzenko, as the house knows, has been given the rights of Canadian citizenship. He is therefore at liberty at any time to discuss any question that he may wish with anyone either in Canada or the United States and either confidentially or otherwise. It is, however, Mr. Gouzenko's own responsibility to determine the effect of any such discussions on the preservation of his new identity, and consequently on his safety. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police have naturally done a great deal to assist Mr. Gouzenko in building up this identity so that the safety of Mr. Gouzenko and his wife and family could be assured without the limitations on their physical freedom that constant guarding might involve.
Mr. Gouzenko has certainly earned the right to this special consideration and assistance as well as to our gratitude by his great services to freedom and the risks he has taken on its behalf. While Mr. Gouzenko then is free to determine his own actions without outside influence, the United States request seems to envisage that the Canadian government itself should make arrangements for an interview or take the responsibility of making Mr. Gouzenko available for questioning by the subcommittee of the United States Senate which I have just mentioned. The Canadian government of course fully appreciate the importance of the closest possible co-operation between the Canadian and United States governments in exchanging information important to the national security of both countries. It has therefore long been our practice, and remains our practice, that security information should be exchanged on a confidential basis, which should be respected
External Affairs
on both sides, between the competent authorities responsible for the internal security of our two neighbouring countries.
In accordance with this principle all information which Mr. Gouzenko has at any time presented to the Canadian government has been placed at the disposal of the responsible United States authorities as it became available. Moreover, facilities are and always have been extended to these competent United States government authorities to clarify any point arising out of any of Mr. Gouzenko's evidence or information at any time they may wish to do so.
The federal bureau of investigation in Washington therefore has always had access to Mr. Gouzenko's special knowledge as and when requested. We have been glad to have for years a liaison officer of the F.B.I. in Ottawa, just as there has been an R.C.M.P. officer in the same capacity in Washington. Mr. Gouzenko has in fact been interviewed on a number of occasions on behalf of the F.B.I., the latest occasion being in August, 1950. In the circumstances therefore I think it is true to say that the benefits of Mr. Gouzenko's special experience with and knowledge of Soviet intelligence organizations and their work have always been made as fully available to the competent United States authorities as to the R.C.M.P. itself. That has been the situation since 1945 and it remains the situation now.
The material secured in this way by the F.B.I. includes information which was not made public in the report of the royal commission on espionage because such information dealt with activities by non-Canadians outside Canadian territory. I emphasize this point, Mr. Speaker, because the second United States request that the government make Mr. Gouzenko available for questioning by the United States Senate subcommittee quotes the chairman of that subcommittee, Senator Jenner, as attaching significance to the fact that the royal commission report did not mention evidence by Mr. Gouzenko that he had heard that an unnamed assistant to the United States secretary of state was a soviet agent.
But this particular piece of evidence, as all other parts of Mr. Gouzenko's evidence and information, was made available to the United States security authorities as it became available to us. Our royal commission, it will be recalled, made a very thorough investigation in secret as a result of which prosecutions were launched, and where those prosecuted under the law were found guilty they were punished, and if found not guilty they were released from custody.

I think it would not have been proper, however, for the Canadian royal commission or the Canadian government to have made public so serious an allegation against an unnamed official of a friendly government. It seemed obvious to us that in accordance with our normal practice in these matters such an allegation should first be investigated by those competent to do so. However, the Canadian government, the Canadian authorities, did pass this testimony confidentially, and I think the house will agree that this was the correct course, to the responsible United States officials.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in addition to these full facilities which I have just mentioned and which have always been available to the F.B.I., the United States government in May, 1B49, requested the Canadian government to arrange for a confidential interview between Mr. Gouzenko and representatives of the immigration subcommittee of the United States Senate committee on the judiciary for the specific purpose of questioning Mr. Gouzenko in relation to certain stated aspects of immigration procedure.
The Canadian government at that time was assured by the United States government that if this request were granted the evidence taken from Mr. Gouzenko would be kept secret unless the Canadian government should agree to its release. Under these circumstances, and under these conditions, the Canadian government then agreed to the United States request, and two members of the staff of the United States Senate subcommittee, to which I have just referred, did come to Ottawa and interviewed Mr. Gouzenko in the presence of a member of the United States embassy and representatives of the R.C.M.P.
The conditions at that time, 1949-they do not seem to be the same now because of the publicity given to this matter-made it possible without too much difficulty for this inquiry of Mr. Gouzenko to be arranged and carried on without the public attention which might, in its turn, have prejudiced Mr. Gouzenko's safety status in this country. I have looked at the evidence again recently, and the questions at this inquiry were not limited to the specific subjects for which the interview had been requested. Of course, we are making no complaint about that. However, nothing beyond the information which Mr. Gouzenko had already made available to the Canadian authorities, and which we made available also at the time to the United States authorities, emerged from this 1949 questioning. In other words, this questioning produced no 
intelligence that had not been already made available to the United States security services.
I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to say a word about the sequence of developments in this matter during the last few weeks. The members of the house will, I think, recall that in October a newspaper which modestly calls itself the world's greatest newspaper, the Chicago Tribune-about that there might, of course, be some difference of opinion- reported an interview with Mr. Gouzenko in which the latter stated that, in his opinion, an interview with a United States congressional committee or members of the United States congress would be, and the words used were, "worth while".
This report was, I think not unnaturally, interpreted by us to mean that Mr. Gouzenko felt he had some further useful information to give. If he had such information or views that were worth while, we naturally thought that he would have given them to us before this or would give them to the Canadian authorities at this time. Immediately this report appeared in the press, therefore, the R.C.M.P. then interviewed Mr. Gouzenko to ascertain whether the report on this matter was accurate and what new information might be secured. An R.C.M.P. officer interviewed Mr. Gouzenko and reported to my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that in the interview of October 27 Mr. Gouzenko had told him he had no information that he had not long since made available to the Canadian authorities; that he had been misquoted by the Chicago Tribune', and that he was not, under any circumstances, willing to proceed to the United States to be interviewed by a congressional committee.
The R.C.M.P. also notified the Minister of Justice that Mr. Gouzenko denied that he had ever criticized the handling of his case by Canadian authorities or the use which was made of the information and documents which he had given to the Canadian authorities. Meanwhile, the Canadian government received the note from the United States Secretary of State transmitting the first request of the Senate subcommittee to interview Mr. Gouzenko, the note of October 29 with which I have already dealt, and the request in this first note was to interview Mr. Gouzenko in Canada.
As the house will recall, because I made a statement at the time in the house, the Canadian government replied that Mr. Gouzenko had stated to the R.C.M.P. that he had been misquoted by the Chicago Tribune and had no additional information to give. The

United States government, therefore, was notified that under the circumstances we assumed that the reasons for the request from the Senate subcommittee had disappeared. I think it was a reasonable assumption to make in view of the interview I have just mentioned between Mr. Gouzenko and the R.C.M.P., but it turned out to be otherwise.
On November 21, I think it was, the same newspaper, the Chicago Tribune, carried another interview with Mr. Gouzenko in which the latter was purported to have upheld the accuracy of the first interview reported in the newspaper on October 25, and to have again expressed the desire for an interview with the United States officials. This made the situation somewhat confusing, and I should like at this point to reaffirm to the house what I said on November 17 last regarding Mr. Gouzenko's statement to the R.C.M.P. It was, of course, on the basis of this statement that the Canadian government prepared its reply to the first request transmitted by the state department. Our reply was delivered on November 4.
This second article to which I have referred in the Chicago Tribune cast some doubt on the R.C.M.P. report, and indeed had some hard things to say about my own good faith and veracity, which are not important enough to trouble the house with. I would merely say that I accept, myself, the accuracy and reliability of that R.C.M.P. report. We have generally found, in this house and in this country, that R.C.M.P. reports are both accurate and reliable.
However, on November 19, the state department delivered another note, a second note, to our ambassador in Washington transmitting a second request from the subcommittee, relating to Mr. Gouzenko, which I have already mentioned. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, whereas the original note from the state department forwarded a request from the subcommittee's counsel to interview Mr. Gouzenko in Canada, the latest note, the second note, forwards a request from the subcommittee chairman this time that Mr. Gouzenko, and I am quoting from it, "be made available for questioning by the subcommittee."
That is in the United States?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It does not say. It just says, "questioning by the subcommittee." Mr. Gouzenko, as I stated, of course is available in that, like any Canadian, he is free to exercise his own judgment to determine his own movements. He can, of course, as I have said, discuss any subject at any time with anyone whom he chooses, and he is the person to
External Affairs
consider the effect of such action on the special measures which have been taken since he came over to us in 1945, in his interests and at his request, to protect him.
The exact purport of the United States note that Mr. Gouzenko be made available for questioning is perhaps not clear, in that it is not explicitly stated where this questioning would take place and under whose responsibility. Presumably, as indeed I have already said, the Canadian government would be expected to take some responsibility in the matter. While I have said that our security authorities do not believe there is any further information to be obtained, the government, in view of this second request from a friendly neighbour, is willing to make arrangements for a meeting to be held under Canadian auspices and in conformity with Canadian procedures. If Mr. Gouzenko is willing to attend at such a meeting, and this is in our note which we gave the United States this afternoon, any person designated by the United States government for this purpose could be present and of course ask questions. It would, of course, Mr. Speaker, have to be understood, and we have made this clear as it was in 1949 at the meeting to which I have already referred, the evidence or information thus secured under the auspices of the Canadian government could not be made public without the approval of that government.
The Canadian government never has attempted and naturally is not now attempting in any way to withhold from competent United States authorities any information that Mr. Gouzenko might have to give and which could in any way strengthen our joint security, or prevent him stating any views he may have on these matters. But we do take the view that any information from a Canadian source on matters of security should be elicited and transmitted to another government in a proper manner in the way which we have in the past found to be very effective and valuable both to ourselves and to our friends, largely because it was done quietly and confidentially.
So, Mr. Speaker, I have now tabled the text of these four communications, which are available to members of the house.
May I now turn for a moment to the second question which was asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) some days ago, and to which he has asked me to reply today. The question: Who in Canada said what, and to whom, about Mr. Harry Dexter White, former assistant secretary of the United States treasury.

External Affairs
Members of the house may have read in the press about a letter from the head of the federal bureau of investigation to a member of the staff of the president of the United States, dated February 1, 1946, which was released by the United States Attorney General, somewhat, as we have already said, to our surprise, as it had been classified and contained references to the Canadian government, and Canadian sources of information.
According to this letter-and I quote from it-
-"sources high placed in the Canadian government" passed information regarding Mr. White's loyalty to his country to the United States authorities.
There has since been considerable public speculation as to who may have passed such information, and what the information was, with a great deal of confusion resulting. The fact, Mr. Speaker, is that the only information which Canadian authorities had on which they could possibly warn our American friends about Mr. White's alleged espionage came from the F.B.I.
We have never secured any information, never been able to secure any information, on this matter from Mr. Gouzenko or any other source. I should explain that following the normal practice governing such cases the federal bureau of investigation, in the winter of 1945-46, informed security authorities in Ottawa that, as a result of information which the F.B.I. had obtained, it appeared that Mr. White might in fact be a soviet agent. Advance advice in such circumstances would allow Canadian security authorities to be on the alert for any evidence of a corroborative nature which they might find here, and none was found.
Now, the initiative taken from Ottawa in this matter was apparently merely designed to make absolutely certain that the F.B.I. were aware that the White about whom they had been making inquiries-the inquiries referred to a moment ago-was in fact the same person whose name was before the United States Senate for confirmation as the United States member of the executive board of directors of the international monetary fund.
The source of this information, this reminder, because that is all it was, and upon which Mr. Hoover appears to have based his letter, was a personal telegram from a security official, not of the Canadian government, but who was stationed in Ottawa to maintain liaison with the Canadian security authorities on behalf of the security services of a friendly third power.
TMr. Pearson.]
It would have in fact been somewhat surprising if this information had been sent by a source high in the Canadian government, because in the report of Mr. Hoover of the F.B.I., which I have mentioned, he stated that this Canadian source on the one hand stated that Canadian delegates to the international monetary fund might nominate and support Mr. White for the office of president -he must have meant executive director of the fund-while on the other hand he said the source had passed on Canadian warnings about White's unfitness on loyalty grounds to hold the post.
While this information, then, did not come from any source in the Canadian government, this non-Canadian source did tell the F.B.I. lhat his message concerning this matter had the blessing of one or two R.C.M.P. security officials with whom it was discussed.
We have done everything possible, Mr. Speaker, to secure the facts on this matter, which include sending a request, to which there has been no reply as yet, to Washington, for the identity of the Canadian source referred to. This we hoped would have provided a quick and easy way of solving the problem. To the best of our knowledge this security liaison officer in Ottawa-not a Canadian-is the source referred to in Mr. Hoover's letter as an official high in the service of the Canadian government. And I should add that this informal message, coming as it did from Ottawa with considerable urgency, might well have been passed on to Mr. Hoover as a Canadian communication, although in fact it was not such.
I should also say for the record that, contrary to statements referred to in Mr. Hoover's letter, at no time did the Canadian government contemplate instructing the Canadian government delegation to support, much less nominate, Mr. White for any post in the international monetary fund, or in any other organization.
It seems clear that in the stress and tension of the moment-and it was a tense and difficult time in Ottawa for security officials -the author of this telegram must have misunderstood the details of information which he had received from some quarter regarding the prospective appointment in the international monetary fund. I find it easy to understand and sympathize with that mistake.
The house may remember the circumstances under which such matters were being dealt with at that particular time. Mr. Gouzenko was being examined in secret in Ottawa, and a distinct but equally important case was being investigated in equal secrecy

in Washington with telegrams and messages about both cases being exchanged between those responsible for security.
It seems clear that the errors in Mr. Hoover's letter concerning the alleged attitude of the Canadian government toward the appointment of Mr. White to a high office in the international monetary fund or the international bank were based upon mistakes originally made in Ottawa in this message from an allied security officer. I must also make it quite clear that this was not a communication in any sense from one government to another. During the war the closest personal working relations developed between the officials of allied countries and it was quite common for responsible persons to communicate informally with each other within their general terms of reference.
The message sent from Ottawa was such a communication, a perfectly proper one, even though inaccurate in one policy point.
Setting the record straight in such detail on this matter has seemed to be necessary to correct the misleading impression caused by uninformed speculations about some alleged high Canadian governmental source apparently being in a position at that time to warn the United States government, on the basis of Canadian intelligence, against some supposed intention of his own government regarding Mr. White.
This statement, Mr. Speaker, and the action which we have now been called to take, will I hope help to dispose of these two matters in a way which recognizes both our responsibility to our own country, our responsibility to co-operate fully with others in our own as well as collective interests, in the effort to defeat and destroy the international communist conspiracy, which is very real and menacing and, finally, our responsibility to do what we can, always, and sincerely, to maintain good relations with our friend and neighbour the United States, the leader and great buttress of the free world. These relations, Mr. Speaker, involve between our two countries many problems of growing complexity. We accept that, but we take I think on both sides of the border deep and abiding satisfaction in the fact that we are able to solve them on the solid basis of mutual friendship, mutual understanding and mutual respect. And I know that, with a few inconsequential exceptions, all Canadians and all Americans, including all hon. members in this house, are anxious to keep it that way.

Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the Leader of the Opposition speaks, and since this is the first occasion that has arisen where a minister has made a statement before the orders of the day are called, I should like to remind hon. members that in the last parliament, when an important statement was made, the leaders of the three opposition parties were permitted to take part in the debate; that is, to ask questions or to make comments. I should like to refer hon. members to page 3669 of Hansard of June 4, 1951, where Mr. Speaker Macdonald said:
It is not customary to allow a debate on a statement made at this stage of the proceedings. I have allowed the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the other two groups to speak, but it is not customary to permit other hon. members to do so.
I should like this gentleman's agreement to be adhered to, if it is possible, following the statement.
And further, on a different occasion, Mr. Speaker Macdonald also ruled that a debate cannot be generalized. He said, as reported at page 411 of Hansard of December 8, 1952:
I think now the house is entering upon a debate on the subject.
It had to do with television policy announced by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). Mr. Speaker Macdonald went on to say:
Of course I cannot allow a debate on it at this time. The remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) should be directed strictly to the statement which has been read. We cannot generalize.
With these previous rulings as a guide, I will ask the Leader of the Opposition to make his comments.

As the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out, this is the first opportunity that he has had to present some of these facts to the house, and I do hope that the statement that has been made may serve to end a great deal of loose speculation that has been appearing in the press and elsewhere, and that can do no good to the relationship between Canada and the United States which is of such vital importance to us and to the whole free world.
May I say on this first opportunity that presents itself, with the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the house, his absence having been due to his duties on behalf of the government, that I do not believe any sensible Canadian thinks for one moment that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has any sympathy whatsoever with communism or would express any sympathy. May I say that

External Affairs
I am sure all of us who recognize the importance of our parliamentary system, whatever our own political affiliation may be, respect government as an institution in this country, and1 resent any suggestion of that kind in relation to the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I do point out that there does seem to have been a great deal of confusion accumulating during the past week.
Some impression seems to have been conveyed that the government of the United States has been reflecting on the conduct of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. No single member of the government has made any comment of any kind that could be interpreted as criticism of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In fact, the only member of the United States government who has spoken or who has said anything on the subject is Mr. Dulles, who referred to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the most complimentary terms. That being so, it would be well if Canadians, here in this chamber and outside, used great care to draw a very clear distinction between responsible statements, and irresponsible statements for which the government of the United States cannot be asked to accept responsibility any more than the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) must be asked to accept responsibility for some irresponsible statements that have been made in this country-and there have been.
It would be well for us to reflect that as we would be inclined to feel some measure of resentment, no matter what party we may support, in regard to criticism of the government of Canada or members of the government of Canada or in fact individuals dealing with public affairs, it is equally likely that people in the United States would have the same feeling.
Perhaps we have all been reminded within the past week of the immense importance in democracies, where we prize free speech, of self-discipline, restraint and a recognition of the fact that once criticisms cross boundaries they may have consequences in no way related to the ordinary criticisms that we offer against each other. We can say quite strong enough things about each other without having to reach outside of Canada to find the target. And the right of free speech, which is inherent in this democracy of ours, will find its full exercise in the appropriate implementing of that freedom by directing those criticisms within our own country to those whose conduct may or may not be affected by what we say. At the moment there is nothing more important in this world in the temporal affairs of every man and woman than the encouragement and

fostering in every way humanly possible of that friendship and understanding which is the one sure uniting influence that will keep the free world together in the face of this immense threat.
Hear, hear.

I would suggest that we might at least hope-and I shall not try to commit the very offence that I was suggesting we should avoid-that in the United States they will remember that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is a member of the Canadian government, appointed by the Canadian government, and that those who wish to maintain friendship with Canada would be well advised to remember that, respecting our governmental system as we do, none of us can disregard those things which might impair respect for that government as an institution. The remarks I make in that regard apply with equal force on this side of the line.
One of the things that I think must perhaps be in the minds of most of us is this: If there can be this much disturbance and the use of this amount of black ink over something which is of such relatively minor importance, I shudder to think of what might happen if the almost unbelievable event occurred that there was some real misunderstanding between Canada and the United States.
Hear, hear.

Surely if there are two peoples in the whole world who can retain a sense of proportion and a true perspective it is these peoples living so close together and understanding each other as well as they do.
Hear, hear.

May I close my remarks by simply expressing my hope that a sense of proportion will be retained and that all of us in Canada, yes, and our friends in the United States, will remember a symbolic event that occurred in this chamber only a week ago Saturday. On that occasion the President of the United States came to us as the head of the most powerful nation in the world, expressing no hint of their belief in power but, on the contrary, expressing his faith in the abiding strength of friendship itself.
I would hope that this will soon be forgotten, that we will retain our perspective, and that we will carry forward that splendid spirit which could be felt in this chamber when President Eisenhower was here such a short time ago.

Mr. Speaker, I think everyone in the house will appreciate the advice that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has given to all members of this house-that they should endeavour to retain a proper perspective concerning the matters that are involved in this particular instance.
However, I would like to go beyond that and say that this house should make it abundantly clear not only that we have confidence in the integrity of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson)- and those of us who have had the privilege of working with him when he was an official of the delegation at San Francisco, and subsequently when he was under-secretary of state for external affairs, know the part that he has taken in these matters-but no one with any sense whatsoever could charge the Secretary of State for External Affairs with having any degree of friendship at all with communism or with the imperial masters of the Soviet union.
I would also like to say that I think this house should back up the position taken by the government of Canada. Obviously the request that came to the government of Canada was that Mr. Gouzenko might be interviewed by a senate committee of the United States on Canadian soil. I think the reply of the Canadian government should meet with the approval of every member of this house and of the public across this country. I think that this country, independent in every respect, could not allow a committee of any other country to establish itself on our soil in order to investigate a Canadian citizen. The government has said, I take if, that if an interview is desired it can be arranged under Canadian auspices, that it can be arranged by Canada, and that the evidence will be submitted to the Canadian government and made available to the other government anxious to have that information.
The thing that shocked me most in connection with this whole matter, and I am very glad to say that it has been partly cleared up this afternoon, was the reference by Mr. Brownell, Attorney General of the United States, who quoted a letter from Mr. Hoover containing information allegedly supplied by a highly placed person in the government of Canada, and which has been referred to as of a "classified" type, and the resultant publicity given to it without first of all consulting Canada.
This afternoon we had a demonstration of how careful the government of Canada is. even when dealing with our own provinces, to secure the consent of the provinces when correspondence that has passed between this 83276-22i
External Affairs
government and the provinces is involved. I sometimes think they go a little beyond reason in that regard. However, I am not saying so this afternoon because it strengthens the fact that the United States Attorney General and Mr. Hoover went beyond the decencies of communication between two countries when the inference was made that this was done by a high official of the Canadian government.
Now, if Mr. Gouzenko wants to testify, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, then-I was going to say he should be permitted but that is wrong-as a Canadian citizen he can go to the United States and testify, but I think it should be made abundantly clear to him that if he goes to the United States to testify he no longer can expect security from the Canadian government or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; and that would relieve us of the substantial expenditure that we are being put to in connection with this gentleman's protection at the present time.
If he wishes to go to the United States let him go; but let the United States then take steps if they wish to do so for his security.
No, no.

We should have nothing further to do with his security if he desires to leave this country, if he cares to let people know who he is and, I suppose, to appear before the television cameras of the United States and all the rest of it. If he does that, then he cannot expect this country to assume responsibility for the maintenance of the veil which Canada has drawn over him in order to protect him. If he rends that veil asunder, then he must assume the consequences. That is my view of the situation at least. I do not want to say more. I rose really because I wanted to say that this house, I think, and the country should support the government in the position that if there is to be any further inquiry of Mr. Gouzenko it will be undertaken under Canadian auspices, if it is on Canadian soil, and under Canadian conditions. I like to think of Canadian conditions as being the conditions that are traditional with our democracy.
I was greatly alarmed in connection with the handling of our espionage investigation in 1946. I am extremely glad that we have not undertaken anything like it since then and I hope we never shall. That is one of the reasons why, whether I am in Canada or elsewhere, if I am asked any questions on what I think of McCarthyism in the United States I shall express myself in terms similar to those used by the hon. member for Spaclina (Mr. Croll) in his effective speech of last Monday.

External Affairs

Mr. Speaker, I think this is an occasion calling for a statement from each of the groups in the house and I am pleased, sir, that you have made it clear that the leaders of the opposition groups would have an opportunity to say a word in reply to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon. May I start in by saying that this group approves the position taken by the government as evidenced by the statement made by the minister this afternoon as it affects Mr. Gouzenko and any statement that he may later make to the representatives of the United States. We think that if Mr. Gouzenko has something that he can contribute in order to help the people of the United States to expose and to root out espionage rings, Canada should, under suitable circumstances, assist him in making a statement. But we support the conditions laid down by the minister that due regard must be had for the security of that man. I think that no one in the house would find much fault with the statement made in that respect this afternoon.
I should like to add, Mr. Speaker, that we Canadians must respect our great neighbour to the south and every effort that they make on their own behalf to render their own security inviolate. It is not our business to try to tell them how they shall conduct their inquiries. It is not our business to criticize the people they put in charge of their inquiries. It is their business. I should like to make it definitely known that I feel it is irresponsible conduct on the part of any Canadian to try to butt into their affairs. Surely if their inquiries are not being conducted as they ought to be conducted, the responsible Americans in the Senate and in congress or elsewhere will take hold of the matter and correct it on their own.
Likewise, I should like to make it definitely clear where I stand with respect to any attempt to interfere in Canadian conduct of inquiries. It is nobody else's business how we want to conduct our inquiries or affairs in Canada. I think that if we are going to have mutual respect and understanding, we have got to have as much restraint in this country as we expect them to have in theirs. I am just afraid that during the past several weeks there have been made on both sides of the line a great many highly emotional and immature statements which ought not to have been made. They have simply added to the confusion and have done nothing else.
I deplore the attacks that have been made by irresponsible people in another nation on

the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I think it was not only unwise and unfair but was certainly most irresponsible. In my association with the minister, although I have disagreed with him on matters of policy, I have never had the slightest doubt of his integrity. I am certain, sir, that we have never at any time felt that the minister had any belief in, or any consort with or sympathy with communists or communism. If we did, we would tell him so here. I should just like to make it known that if there is any suspicion about the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we in Canada feel that we can deal with it and we do not have to wait for anybody in any other land to bring it to our attention or to help us to do it. I believe in our rights and I believe in people respecting our rights. I also feel that we ought to be prepared to respect theirs in the same manner.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON REDUCTION OF FLOOD HAZARD
speechtext: I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Public Works. Was the final report entitled "Reduction of the flood hazard in the greater Winnipeg area" submitted to the Manitoba government for consideration? Also, will a copy be officially tabled in this house and, if so, will copies be made available to the members?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON REDUCTION OF FLOOD HAZARD
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. In reply I would say that the final report of the investigation into measures for the reduction of the flood hazard in the greater Winnipeg area, prepared by the Department of Resources and Development, was transmitted to the premier of Manitoba with my letter of September 25, 1953. The report consists of eight rather voluminous appendices and a summary which sets forth in a concise way the general problem and possible solutions. The report is in mimeographed form. Printing would take some months and cost a considerable sum of money. However, a limited number of copies of the report and appendices are available. Because, in my opinion, it is a good report which will add to the public fund of knowledge on flooding generally, I shall be pleased to see that a copy is tabled tomorrow and that as many copies as possible will be forwarded to the distribution office.
I would emphasize that this is not a government report which there is any obligation to table. Rather it is a report prepared by

departmental officials. I should not like my action in this case to be construed in the future as a precedent with respect to the tabling of such departmental reports.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night, I was suggesting to the government an amendment to the Criminal Code which would allow a national lottery. I have given the main reasons which, in my opinion, justify such an amendment to our Criminal Code. I have no intention of repeating them, but I cannot leave the matter without setting at rest the minds of die-hard autonomists. In proposing such a national lottery it is not my intention to suggest that there should be the least infringement upon the rights of any province.
Such an amendment to the Criminal Code authorizing a lottery would enable the provinces wishing to do so to organize their own lotteries without getting into trouble. I believe that a national lottery would create a genuine interest among the people. An agreement could be reached between the various provinces wishing to organize such a lottery and the central authorities so that the new system could operate in conformity with the views of all provinces concerned and of the Canadian government.
I have completed my remarks on the subject. If you permit me, I would like to devote the few minutes that remain at my disposal to make to the government some suggestions with a view to improving the situation of my fellow citizens.
Before going any further, I deem it a duty to congratulate sincerely my colleagues of the house who have called the government's attention to the precarious situation of the textile industry at present. I believe I have read somewhere that the government intends to take steps to help that industry which employs thousands of people throughout the country and especially in the province of Quebec, where I live.
I spoke previously of another industry, the fur industry. I then asked the government to examine the advisability of levying a tax on raw furs exported to the United States, the surplus of which is shipped back to Canada
The Address-Mr. Dupuis at a dumping price after it has been processed, as in the case of textiles; under present circumstances such a procedure is disastrous to the industry as well as to fur manufacturers in our country. I wonder if the government is studying that question. I do believe that this industry is important enough to warrant some measure to alleviate the present conditions, as has been advocated for the textile industry.
I have already referred to other questions about which I would like to say a few more words, but I have not the time to do so. I notice, for instance, that several of our friends, more particularly those on the opposite side of this house, have raised the question of whether it would be advisable to increase family allowances and old age pensions. Like all other members of this house, no doubt, I receive many letters telling me that the present rate of family allowances; and old age pensions, due to the high cost of living, is now lower than the rate which was set when these measures were adopted.
I am not unaware of what the Department of National Health and Welfare has accomplished, so far, in the social field. I am also acquainted with the efforts which this department has made to keep up with the times, to follow the social evolution which we are witnessing today. I am convinced that the Department of National Health and Welfare, the government itself, even its leader-though I have no right to speak in the name of the Prime Minister-have this matter under serious consideration. As soon as circumstances allow it is to be hoped that some improvement will be made in this regard.
We must not forget, though, as the Prime Minister himself remarked, that it is not difficult to promise the people the moon and the stars-I am not quoting exactly-to increase the social benefits already provided under the different acts. All that is very well, but, as he also remarked, we must also have adequate sources of revenue to cover increased expenditures. I am sure that when the amounts we are called upon to spend for our national defence-and those are absolutely necessary expenditures which have never been criticized by any member of this house-are decreased because of sufficient improvement in the international situation, we will also consider bringing further improvement to our own conditions, by increasing the various allowances granted in the social field, if it be deemed necessary. Everything now seems to indicate that this is probable.
It would also be desirable-and this is mentioned in the speech from the throne- to consider with a liberal and generous mind the lot of those we call the handicapped, or

I have been pleased to notice that the government intends to give particular attention to this category of unfortunate people, and I know that, in due time, this house will be asked to consider a bill providing for valuable assistance to these people.
There are several other suggestions we could make before the budget is drafted. Last night, I said that after the budget speech it would be too late to make our suggestions. Therefore we should make our suggestions now. I beg the government to find a way of decreasing further the tax on tobacco in general, not only on cigarettes, even though the only aim would be to discourage smuggling. I will not repeat all that has been said in favour of the lowering of that tax, but I wish to repeat my request as far as leaf tobacco and cigarette tobacco are concerned.
In my humble opinion, the man who takes the trouble of rolling his own cigarettes, as we say, is still paying too high a tax. I sincerely believe that the Minister of Finance <Mr. Abbott) will give special attention to that part of his budget speech that deals with the excise tax on cigarettes and, more particularly, on cigarette tobacco and leaf tobacco.
As my time is up, I repeat, in conclusion, that I hope the toll on the Jacques Cartier bridge will be removed in the very near future for the benefit of the citizens of Montreal and the south shore. I do not want to trouble the government with that question, but, on the other hand-and I have placed a notice of motion on the order paper in this connection-I believe that it would be a wise move to study the opportunity of coming to an agreement with the government of the province of Quebec on the removal of the toll on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges.
I know that the city of Montreal was reluctant to live up to its obligations; it refused to pay its share of the deficit under the agreement passed between the federal government, the provincial government and the city. I also know that the province of Quebec still owes a substantial sum of money, and I hope that the federal government will not be compelled to sue for payment, as that province was itself compelled to sue the city of Montreal to obtain payment.
I understand that there is still a substantial sum owing by the province. I believe that the holding of a meeting such as the one I have suggested would not only bring about a settlement of old debts but would allow

for the negotiating of new conditions as far as the two parties to the contract are concerned.
I would have liked to discuss this matter at greater length. I know that the federal government is well disposed in this regard. On the other hand we must also recognize that respect for contracts is not merely the federal government's responsibility but that it is also that of the provincial authorities who should carry out the provisions of the contract before proclaiming, in public meetings, that the federal government is responsible for the fact that toll charges are collected on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges, since this matter comes under their jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, I now bring my remarks to a close. I already told you at the outset how all those questions of great economic importance had been brought to the attention of the electors as a whole. I also recalled the wonderful promises made by a certain party leader while, at the same time, I spoke of that appeal to autonomy made by the government's opponents. Judgment has been passed on all those things.
I now conclude by expressing the wish that the twenty-second parliament will know how to maintain this prosperity, this unprecedented economic impetus, this industrial development, in a word, the prosperity of this country.
I congratulate the right hon. the Prime Minister on his progressive policy which has made of this country a pleasant land to live in. I do not doubt in the least that Providence will keep him at the helm for a long time to come, for the greatest good of all Canadians.

The debate in reply to the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, has been going on now for some time. At this point I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and seconder (Mr. Villeneuve), and more particularly all the other new members who have come into the house as a result of the recent election who have taken part in this debate. Those of us who have been in the house for some time do receive new points of view from those who rise at different times to speak in the early sessions following an election, and those who have spoken on this occasion have given us a great deal of food for thought in relation to many matters which will be discussed here from time to time.

On this occasion, however, I wish to express my appreciation particularly to the official opposition and the C.C.F. party. They have, as has been their custom, moved amendments to the address. I am going to read the main amendment moved by the official opposition, which is found on page 43 of Hansard for November 16, 1953:
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that the welfare of Canada is dependent upon free competition; and that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade.
This amendment is so differently worded from those to which I have been accustomed since coming to Ottawa that I really must express appreciation to the official opposition for the wording of it. While it does make a passing reference to agriculture by mentioning the restoration of markets for primary products-I suppose some would argue that that does cover the question to a degree-still this amendment is so different from those moved at other sessions when care was taken to condemn everything that related to agricultural policy that I must express my own appreciation to the official opposition for having worded this particular amendment in the manner in which they have.
Then I should probably express my appreciation of the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party which is found on page 56 of Hansard for November 16, 1953:
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade.
That is the Conservative amendment, and to that is added these words:
We further represent that this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation.
Again, in the wording of this amendment there has not been the usual criticism. I think both the official opposition and the C.C.F. have given expression to the view generally held right across Canada with regard to agricultural policy, which is to the effect that agriculture is in a better position, not only in relation to other activities within Canada but in relation to activities outside Canada, than it has been on many previous occasions.

The suggestion that I expressed any other idea, of course, is very wide of the mark. I have here on my desk all the documents which were submitted to the conference, and they clearly express the opinion that, in so far as agriculture is concerned, as compared with the years that have preceded this, it is in a very good position.
In order to make the position clear I should like to say that we began to discuss the possible future of agriculture in Canada at the end of the war. At that time great fear was expressed that we were going to have, at a very early date, a depression similar to that which we had immediately following the first world war, and possibly one that would even match the depression of the thirties. We have gone along since that time, and I do not think there is any member in this house who would suggest that we have had anything akin to the situation about which fears were expressed at that time.
I have before me a summary of the happenings of the last five years which bears out the statements that have been made in the conference during the last two days, to which reference was made by the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). In statements made there it was suggested time after time that there had been a very considerable increase in returns' for farm products in the years 1951 and 1952, and that there had been some reduction in 1953 as compared with the other years. On each occasion it was suggested, however, that there were some remarkable circumstances associated with 1951 and 1952 which could not be associated with any other years.
As I look back over the records I find there was a constant increase in the returns to farmers, both gross and net, in all the years from the end of the war down to 1949. In every year there was an increase in returns, both in total amount and in the prices received for products. In 1949 the cash receipts from the sale of farm products, that is gross receipts, amounted to $2,486 million. Taking that as 100, the returns in 1950 were $2,213 million or 89 per cent; that is there was a reduction of 11 per cent as between 1949 and 1950.
336	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gardiner
As I remember the discussions which took place in this house at that time, it was suggested that we were on the way down; that we were going to continue on the way down, and that eventually we would have in this country conditions very similar to those we had in the depression periods following other wars. But in 1951 the gross cash return was $2,812 million, or 113 per cent of what it had been in 1949. Then in 1952 it was $2,778 million or 112 per cent of what it was in 1949.
This brings me down to 1953. The Current Review which has been quoted by a number of members in this debate is the current review for November, and most of the material in it was compiled up to about September. So any references made there are only with regard to returns that had come in in connection with agriculture down to that time. But when you take the figures available now, and use those as a basis for the estimate for this year, the total cash return is $2,660 million; and its relation to 1949 is expressed by the figure 107 as against 100 in 1949.

speechtext: Has the minister the figures for net farm income?

Yes, I shall give those. I have them here, along with the others. They really express a similar position, although in slightly different terms. On each occasion that reference is made to the cash returns of farmers, the question just asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) is asked by someone. We are asked: Have you the net returns, too? I realize there is a difference between net and gross returns; but I am also of the opinion that the farmer who understands what net returns, as against gross returns, actually means is not nearly so afraid as some of those who do not actually have farm products of their own.
The figures compiled to indicate net returns take into consideration the fact that last year we had a higher production of wheat in western Canada than we had this year. They say that, because we had a higher production of wheat last year than we had this year, and therefore not so much to carry over from this year's crop as we carried over from last year's, our net position is not as good this year as it was last year.
Well, our net position as to cash returns for the present year may not be as good; but in so far as my farm is concerned, in view of the fact that I have not been able to market all my crop of last year and that a very considerable part of it is still on my


farm, and further in view of the fact that I had a very good crop this year I, and I am sure other farmers in western Canada, actually have more grain on our farms today than we ever had at any other time. And no one is able to convince us that because we have that grain on the farms we are worse off than we were last year, or worse off than we were the year before, or five years before that. We are not worse off with those supplies of grain piled up on our farms than we were before, and no farmer believes that we are.

It is pertinent; but I am
sure that after I have finished my hon. friend can apply those points in any way he wishes to have them applied, and draw his conclusions accordingly. In so far as these particular figures are concerned they indicate something which I think members of the house should keep in mind when they are discussing the question. Because if they do not, farmers outside certainly do.

These figures indicate that our prices in 1951 took a turn to a higher level, after having dropped considerably in 1950. There are a number of reasons as to why they took that turn. I am not going to discuss them this afternoon because it might require me to offer some opinions which would not be in accordance with the opinions suggested a few moments ago by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew).
If we were going to go into a discussion of why we had such great price increases in 1951 as compared with 1950, we would have to step outside this country to give those reasons, and perhaps offer some criticism as to the manner in which they were brought about. Then again, I would call attention to the fact that prices for farm commodities in that year were very high. We got from 32 to 34 cents a pound for our beef cattle, slightly under 30 cents for our hogs, a fairly high price for our cheese, and a price for our butter which was comparable with that we still obtain. And for other farm products such as wheat, barley and oats we had very high prices.
What I wish to say here today-and it is a repetition of what I said at the conference to which the hon. member for Mackenzie referred a few moments ago-is that I have travelled back and forth across this country a great deal, and I have never yet met a farmer who has intimated to me that he expected over any period of time to get the prices he received in 1951 for his livestock. I have met farmers who think that probably the price of wheat ought to stay very much around the price it has been for the last ten years, but I have not met any who have suggested that we could hope to maintain cattle prices at their 1951 level.
Then again, going across the country, I have not met any farmers who have suggested to me that the unusually high prices we have obtained for hogs in 1953 are always going to continue, or that they are going to continue for any considerable length of time. In other words the arguments put up here that we have had a reduction in prices of farm commodities, and a slight reduction in gross returns, or in net returns, are not arguments which appeal to farmers in general. They have their situation well in hand, and know pretty well what it is.
In discussing farm commodities in relation to the questions that have been put up here, and were put up for the last two days in the conference, it is necessary for us to divide farm commodities into two classifications. One is those that are produced largely in, let us say, one province, or some like potatoes may be produced largely in two provinces such as New Brunswick and Prince Edward
The Address-Mr. Gardiner Island, so far as they are produced for marketing purposes. Then we have other commodities like apples produced in Ontario and Quebec, it is true, but with a market right at the door of the farmer for all that are produced there. But we also have a production in Nova Scotia and British Columbia where the market is not so easily available, and where all agree that one of the essential features of any policies of the future should be a return of the British market for apples from these two areas particularly in order that they might at all times have access to a market where they can sell their product.
Having said that, I should like to point out that we have followed a policy ever since 1939 in relation to that particular matter. When the people of Prince Edward Island come and ask us to do something about potatoes we point out to them that if this government centralized the promotion of potato production at Ottawa and took action right across Canada which would be beneficial to the people of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, we would harm the potato producers of those two provinces and not help them. And when they come here to discuss the question they are satisfied that that is true. Both those provinces are now utilizing the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939, which we put on the statute books at that early date in order to deal with just such questions as these. I hold in my hand a list of those who have come under that act within the last year. Farmers have been utilizing the act for the purpose for which it was intended, namely in connection with products which are produced in certain limited areas for which they must find markets and cannot find markets. They have been using that act. Prince Edward Island has the ranch-bred fox pelts organization operating under that act.

In Ontario we have an agreement with the Ontario cheese producers' association under which we guarantee advances in connection with the marketing of cheddar cheese.

In Saskatchewan-and these are only the ones that came in in the last year; they have been coming in constantly since 1939, but this group came in within the last year-we have forage crops seeds; the Saskatchewan Forage Crop Co-operative Marketing Association Limited of Prince Albert; then the Alberta forage crop seeds, the Alberta seed growers' co-operative, at Edmonton, and the forage crop seeds in Alberta again. You ask me, what is the nature of that legislation? I say, well, the legislation is based on the experience we have had in selling many farm products under co-operatives. Therefore they go ahead and promote their own production to their heart's content, and they go on and market the product which has been produced as the result of their activities and we, through our guarantee, make it possible for them to finance their operation.
